notes: CONFIRMED 2026-09-12, design note E.140: Perrett & Laurier's Panzerkampfwagen IV Medium Tank 1936-1945 (Osprey) gives a labeled technical cutaway diagram (pp.26-27) with callouts matching this figure exactly, twice ('Front armour plate 80mm' and '80mm superstructure armour plate' for the lower and upper hull-front plates respectively), independently corroborated by body text (pp.8, 14: '80mm integral front armour'). The word 'integral' is doing real work: the same book explicitly contrasts this against the preceding Ausf G's 30mm bolt-on appliqué construction, confirming Ausf H's 80mm is a SINGLE plate, not a layered composite like StuG III's own recently-corrected hull front (E.138) -- do not apply that same layered-plate correction here, it was specific to the Ausf-G-style bolt-on construction this vehicle did not use. face_hardened=True traces to Bird & Livingston Ch.3 (a general claim naming Ausf H specifically for 'thicker plates' beyond the 30-50mm policy bracket); this pass found a real but DIFFERENT face-hardening claim in the same new book (a 1942 British evaluation of a captured Ausf E's MG-mounting/port covers specifically, not the Ausf H's own glacis) -- not a contradiction, but not an independent re-confirmation of the existing claim either, recorded as a nuance. One unresolved data point from the same diagram, not incorporated: callout 3, '20mm armour glasis plate,' doesn't match any figure this project has and its exact location on the vehicle couldn't be pinned down at this pass's scan resolution -- flagged, not guessed at. See counters/toe/panzer4_ausfh_verification_1943.md.

Hull roof, ~10mm -- three independent secondary sources converge (Wikipedia infobox citing Chris Conners' AFV Database, tanks-encyclopedia.com, historyofwar.org) but none is a page-cited primary source. Top AV is modeled as a flat, unsloped plate (vertical_deg=0) -- it represents the plate's raw resistance to a near-perpendicular hit (mortars/artillery falling close to vertical, or the worst-case exposure angle under the Sidehill Exposure optional rule, Rule 18.2c), not the near-90-degree obliquity a normal horizontal shot sees against a flat deck. See counters/toe/vehicle_top_armor_1943.md.

Turret roof: 10mm on early Ausf H production, reinforced mid-production to 16-25mm segments (Jentz & Doyle, Panzer Tracts No. 4, p.50 -- the best-cited figure in the whole top-armor research pass). Using 16mm as representative of 1943 production, since most 1943 output postdates the reinforcement. See counters/toe/vehicle_top_armor_1943.md.

Layered composite: 20mm bolted applique + 50mm base plate, computed via layered_plate_effective_thickness(first_hit_mm=20, underlying_mm=50)=56.0mm (Ch.9 p.38 formula, validated against the chapter's own 3 worked examples this session). face_hardened_fraction=50/70=0.714 reflects that only the base plate (within the confirmed 30-50mm 1942 policy bracket) is face-hardened, not the bolt-on applique -- blended via ArmorPlate.face_hardened_fraction rather than the all-or-nothing face_hardened flag. This project's own construction (how to blend partial face-hardening), not directly sourced -- see design spec S17/19. heat_thickness_mm/heat_vertical_deg overridden to the raw 70mm/21deg: Ch.9's layered-plate discount is derived from kinetic plugging-shear test data and there is no sourced basis for applying the same discount to a HEAT jet's penetration mechanism -- deliberately NOT applying the kinetic-specific correction to HEAT rather than assuming it carries over.

schurzen: standard running-production feature on PzIII/PzIV from ~March 1943, within this vehicle's 1943 era -- external general knowledge, not confirmed in either project source (searched, not found)

Ch.20 p.88 (confirmed verbatim this session): 'British firing tests against Tiger E armor in North Africa indicated that the 310-330 Brinell side armor resisted penetration with the same resistance as good quality Allied test plate.' No schurzen: Thoma-shield turret skirts were a ~spring-1944 field feature, after this vehicle's 1943 era
same plate class as side, applying same measured BHN

pre-resolved via Ch.10 mantlet edge-effect table (p.42), 76mm-class attacker, combined mantlet+turret-front-bar resistance. CONFIRMED 2026-09-12, design note E.134: a direct read of Ch.10's own table gives 143mm for the 76mm-class row exactly, an exact match to this project's existing figure -- no correction needed, but the table also has other calibers this project's own roster fields against Tiger and this vehicle only ever prints one flat override regardless of attacker caliber. Full table (mm resistance vs. capped/APBC-family attackers): 57mm=157, 75/76mm=143 (this row), 85mm=139, 90mm=139, 100mm=133, 122mm=119, 152mm=104. A separate AP-family column: 85mm=142, 100mm=135, 122mm=121, 152mm=105. This project's 57mm-class guns (6pdr) and 85mm-class guns (Soviet D-5T) would see a real, currently-uncaptured difference (157mm and 139mm respectively) if ever checked against this exact plate -- resolve_av()'s override mechanism only supports one flat value per plate, not a caliber-keyed table, so this is recorded here as reference data for a future matchup check or mechanism extension, not yet built into the pipeline.
Hull top (roof+floor, undifferentiated by the source) = 25mm. Jentz & Doyle 1993 pp.8/16, corroborated by Hart 2007 p.17. See counters/toe/vehicle_top_armor_1943.md.

CORRECTED 2026-09-12, design note E.138: Panzer Tracts No.8 (Jentz & Doyle), the authoritative primary source for this exact vehicle, states plainly (p.8-26) that the Ausf.G's frontal armor is '50 mm base plate with 30 mm face-hardened plates bolted on' -- directly answering the question this row's own note previously declined to guess at. Layered composite: 30mm bolted face-hardened applique + 50mm base plate (unhardened), computed via layered_plate_effective_thickness(first_hit_mm=30, underlying_mm=50)=64.2mm, same Ch.9 p.38 formula and methodology already used for Panzer III's own hull front. face_hardened_fraction=30/80=0.375 reflects that only the applique layer (not the base plate) is face-hardened -- the OPPOSITE arrangement from Panzer III's own layered plate (where the base, not the applique, was the hardened layer); blended via ArmorPlate.face_hardened_fraction, same construction as that row. AV-vs-Capped (75mm reference) moves from 87.1mm (old single-80mm-plate model) to 64.0mm (new layered model) -- a real, substantial reduction, not a rounding change; checked against this roster's only StuG III Rule 18.12 entry (StuG III vs T-34 Model 1943) and found no effect, since StuG III is the shooter in that matchup, not the target. heat_thickness_mm/heat_vertical_deg overridden to the raw 80mm/21deg, same reasoning as Panzer III's row: Ch.9's layered-plate discount is derived from kinetic plugging-shear data with no sourced basis for a HEAT jet. Independently corroborated 2026-09-12 by a second book (Doyle & Jentz, Sturmgeschutz III Assault Gun 1940-42, p.38): 'bolting on additional armour with cylindrical bolts... continued to the end of the war with every Sturmgeschutz Ausf.G' -- confirms the general bolt-on mechanism for this exact variant from a second, independent source, though it gives no thickness figures of its own and so doesn't refine the numbers above. See counters/toe/stug3_panzer_tracts_1943.md and counters/toe/stug3_osprey_1940_42_1943.md.

CORRECTED 2026-09-12, design note E.133: a direct read of Bird & Livingston Ch.6 (this project's own foundational armor-ballistics source, previously only cited secondhand via Wikipedia) gives a worked example directly on this vehicle -- 'The M4A1 had an all-cast hull and mid-glacis armor was 51mm at 53 degrees,' with a medium flaw multiplier applied, contrasted explicitly against the unflawed post-October-1943 63.5mm@47deg redesign. The previous figure (51mm@47deg, no flaw) was neither of the book's own two documented M4-series configurations -- it mixed the pre-fix thickness with the post-fix angle and applied no flaw correction either way, with no independent citation for the 47deg figure ever recorded in this project. This also resolves design note E.126's 'honest non-finding' on the Sherman glacis QC question: the book's Ch.6 opens with the exact sentence that research pass searched for and couldn't find ('Prior to October, 1943, American armor production and quality control permitted flawed armor to occur in many tanks, which includes almost all 56 degree glacis Shermans') -- it was in this project's own primary source all along, just never read directly until now. Net effect on AV-vs-Capped (75mm reference diameter): 76.7mm (old) -> 79.7mm (new) -- the steeper angle's slope benefit outweighs the flaw penalty. cast=True unchanged (still an all-cast hull); cast_deficiency_multiplier still applies on top, unrelated to this correction. See counters/toe/sherman_glacis_qc_1943.md and design note E.133.

Isigny-measured actual glacis (85mm@57deg), not nominal 80mm@55deg, per Ch.6's own recommendation. Slope-only cross-validated against source's own parallel 76mm-vs-glacis calc (236-248mm). Medium flaw multiplier applied (Ch.6) -- cross-validated against two of the chapter's own Panther-glacis worked examples (152mm APBC and 17pdr APCBC, both within ~1%). 'Medium' chosen as representative since Ch.14's own table note (p.66, precise citation added 2026-09-12 per design note E.134 -- a direct read confirmed this is Ch.14, not Appendix 5, which instead covers Panther's non-glacis areas and found them unflawed) states about half of Panthers had flawed glacis armor starting summer 1944; not a claim every glacis is exactly medium-flawed. Dating note added 2026-09-12: the book's own flaw statistic is specifically pinned to 'starting summer 1944' production, while this roster dates Panther Ausf G to 1943 (Ausf G production itself historically began March 1944) -- an existing project convention predating this note, not newly introduced by it, but flagged here since the flaw statistic's own dating sits right at the edge of that convention rather than comfortably inside this project's 1943 window.

SOURCED, found this session: Ch.14 'Armor Data for Selected Vehicles' (printed p.66), never previously read -- Appendix 5 doesn't cover rear-hull data but Ch.14 does. Ch.11 Panther-mantlet angle-probability distribution (pp.43-45: 65-75:20%, 50-60:31.2%, 35-45:24.8%, 20-30:14.4%, 0-15:9.6%) -- CONFIRMED 2026-09-12, design note E.134: a direct read of Ch.11 matches this distribution exactly, to the tenth of a percent. Weighted-averaged against 100mm apex thickness (cast) -- methodology is this project's own construction applied to sourced data; Ch.11 gives hit-angle probabilities only, not a Tiger-style pre-computed combined-resistance table, so this project's own weighting is still the best available treatment, now built on a confirmed-accurate input distribution rather than an unverified one. NEW FINDING (Ch.14, printed p.66, found 2026-09-11): the table lists 'Mantlet: 100c rounded' AND, as a SEPARATE row, 'Turret Front: 110c @ 10' for Panther G -- possibly indicating an additional turret front plate behind/around the mantlet casting, similar in concept to Tiger's separate 'turret front bar' behind its mantlet (Ch.10). This AV figure (249.2mm) only ever accounted for the mantlet itself -- if a genuinely separate 110mm@10deg turret front plate also exists, this figure may be UNDERSTATED. RECONFIRMED 2026-09-12: an independent second direct read of Ch.14 found the same two-row listing again, ruling out a first-pass misreading -- this is a real, repeatedly-observed feature of the primary source, not an artifact. Still not chased down (how the mantlet and this separate plate combine is not stated in either read) -- flagged for a dedicated follow-up, not guessed at.

Uppermost of a 3-plate stepped glacis; the middle (57mm) and lower (140mm) plates have sourced thicknesses. Using the well-cited, fully-vertical 152mm plate as the single Hull Front representative value continues to understate whatever slope the lower plates genuinely have; the lower plate's now-known angle is recorded here as known-but-not-yet-incorporated pending the middle plate's own angle. CAVEAT ADDED 2026-09-12, design note E.137: a direct read of the actual Fletcher & Harley (2006) 'Cromwell Cruiser Tank 1942-50' book (now in the project's reference material) could not confirm this citation -- p.12 as read contains general design/production narrative, no turret-armor thickness figure, and no 76.7mm or 64mm figure was found anywhere in the book's 50 pages. This does not disprove 76.7mm (the citation may point to a different edition/printing with different pagination, or the original citation may have been to Wikipedia's own infobox rather than a verified direct page read), but the 'direct page citation' framing above should be treated as unconfirmed, not stronger evidence than the uncited alternatives it was originally preferred over. Small-hatch M4A4 ('Sherman V') glacis: 51mm at 56deg from vertical -- M4A4 production (1942-Sept 1943) never received the later large-hatch hull upgrade this project's existing M4A3(76mm) row uses (64mm@47deg), per Sherman Tank Site ('the A4 version never got the improved large hatch hull'). The exact 51mm/56deg pairing is corroborated only at forum level, not against a page-cited primary -- treat the hull generation (small-hatch, not large-hatch) as solid, the exact figure as probable-but-not-independently-verified. Welded construction (Wikipedia, Sherman Tank Site both describe the M4A4 hull as welded, correcting an earlier assumption of riveted construction). 1944-dated: outside this project's usual 1943 baseline (Firefly entered British service ~Jan 1944, combat debut Normandy June 1944). See counters/toe/sherman_firefly_1944.md.

38mm, inferred by extension from this project's existing M4A1/M4A3 rows (both 38mm) and general Sherman literature -- not independently confirmed for the M4A4 hull specifically by any source found. Genuinely an open figure, not a citation. See counters/toe/sherman_firefly_1944.md.

Standard M4 turret casting reused (not a new turret design) with a new mantlet specifically credited with '+13mm of protection added' over the standard Sherman mantlet (Wikipedia, footnoted to Fletcher, Sherman Firefly, Osprey New Vanguard 141 -- the single best-cited figure in this research pass). Modeled as this project's existing Sherman M4A1 turret-front av_override_mm (89mm, itself a weighted mantlet hit-distribution average, Ch.8) plus that sourced +13mm delta = 102mm -- a deliberate, documented stand-in rather than a fresh hit-distribution re-weighting for the Firefly's own differently-shaped mantlet, which would need source data not available this session. Wikipedia's own uncited '89mm maximum' infobox figure for Firefly turret front coincidentally matches the M4A1 number and is explicitly NOT the basis for this figure -- flagged to avoid that coincidence being mistaken for corroboration. See counters/toe/sherman_firefly_1944.md.

51mm, same as this project's existing M4A1 turret side/rear figure -- three independent sources agree the Firefly reused the standard M4 turret casting with no wall-thickness change; only the gun/recoil system, mantlet, radio bustle, and loader's hatch were modified. See counters/toe/sherman_firefly_1944.md.

62mm -- NOT the base turret's original rear wall, but the armoured radio bustle box added to house the radio relocated out of the hull (Sherman Minutia: bustle sides 51mm, rear 62mm). A genuine, sourced improvement over the base turret's 51mm rear wall, not a guess -- the bustle is a real armoured structure bolted/welded on, not a report of the original wall being thinned.
